2027-02-28.title: Third Sunday of Lent
readings: The law was given through Moses
Lord, you have the words of everlasting life
We proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles
Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up
2027-02-28.alt: Year B. Where there are catechumens, the Year A readings may be used every year, and they are always used at a Mass with the First Scrutiny of the elect: Exodus 17:3–7; Psalm 95:1–2, 6–7, 8–9 (If today you hear his voice, harden not your hearts); Romans 5:1–2, 5–8; John 4:5–42 (the Samaritan woman at the well). No Gloria. Liturgical colour: violet.
2027-02-28.verse: Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
theo: On the Third Sunday of Lent Year B places two great signs side by side: the Law given on Sinai and the Temple cleansed in Jerusalem. The first reading begins not with a command but with a reminder of grace: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” Only then come the Ten Words: no other gods, no idols, no misuse of God's name, keep holy the sabbath, honour father and mother, do not kill, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness or covet. The commandments are not chains placed on slaves; they are the way of life for a people already set free. That is why the Psalm can sing that the law of the LORD is “perfect, reviving the soul,” more to be desired than gold, “sweeter also than honey.” The Church's response puts Peter's words on our lips: “Lord, you have the words of everlasting life.”

In the Gospel Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for the Passover and finds the Temple courts turned into a market: oxen, sheep and doves for sale, money changers at their tables. “Making a whip of cords, he drove all of them out of the temple,” poured out the coins and overturned the tables: “Stop making my Father's house a marketplace!” The disciples remember the Psalm: “Zeal for your house will consume me.” This is not a loss of temper; it is a prophetic sign. Malachi had promised that the Lord would suddenly come to his temple to purify it, and now he has come. When the leaders demand a sign, Jesus gives a riddle: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” They think of the stone building, forty-six years in the making. “But he was speaking of the temple of his body.” The true meeting place of God and humanity is no longer a building but the Body of Christ, destroyed on the cross and raised on the third day. Through baptism we are built into that Body; we become, in St Paul's words, God's temple.

St Paul tells us what sign we preach: “Jews demand signs and Greeks desire wisdom, but we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to those who are the called… Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.” The cross looks like weakness and folly, yet “God's foolishness is wiser than human wisdom, and God's weakness is stronger than human strength.” Lent is the time to let Jesus cleanse the temple of our hearts: to overturn the tables where we bargain with God, drive out the idols of money, pleasure and pride, and keep his commandments with love. Where there are catechumens, the Church today reads the Year A Gospel of the Samaritan woman at the well and celebrates the First Scrutiny, praying that the elect may be freed from what is weak and sinful and filled with the living water of Christ. Both Gospels lead to the same place: the new temple, from which living water flows, is Jesus himself.
conn: In Hebrew the commandments are called “the ten words” (Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13). They were written on two tablets: love of God and love of neighbour (Catechism 2067).
John's Gospel mentions three Passovers in the ministry of Jesus; he places the cleansing of the Temple at the beginning, as a key to everything that follows.
Pilgrims had to pay the Temple tax in Tyrian silver; changers set up their tables in the Court of the Gentiles, the only place where non-Jews could pray.
Herod the Great began rebuilding the Temple about 20 BC; the work went on long after his death. It was destroyed by the Romans in AD 70.
Psalm 69:9; the psalm of the suffering righteous one. The zeal that consumes Jesus will lead him to the cross.

On the Third, Fourth and Fifth Sundays of Lent the elect receive the scrutinies, with the Gospels of the Samaritan woman, the man born blind and Lazarus (Year A), prayers of healing and exorcism before Easter Baptism.
altar: Jesus said: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. At the altar we receive that risen Body, the true temple, and become what we receive.
The church building is holy because it is the house where Christ's Body gathers and his sacrifice is offered. We keep it a house of prayer, not a market.

live: Examine yourself by the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20)
Use the commandments for an examination of conscience this week, and go to confession.
Remove one thing from your life, phone or home that pushes God out.
Come early to Mass, keep silence in church, and let it be a house of prayer.
Pray for the catechumens at their scrutinies, that Christ may free and fill them.
fathers: Those who sell in the temple are those who seek their own things in the Church, not the things of Jesus Christ. Let zeal for God's house consume every Christian: if you see a brother going astray, do what you can to call him back.
The Lord did not abolish the natural precepts of the law contained in the Ten Commandments; he extended and fulfilled them, calling us to follow them as sons and daughters, not as slaves.
The cross, which seemed foolish and weak, won over the whole world through unlettered fishermen. What looked like defeat was the power of God.

saints: Armenian monk of the monastery of Narek (about 950–1005), mystic and poet, author of the Book of Lamentations, ninety-five prayers “speaking with God from the depths of the heart.” Declared a Doctor of the Church in 2015.
1–6 Mar: Lenten weekdays of the third week. 4 Mar: St Casimir (commemoration). 7 Mar: Fourth Sunday of Lent (Laetare); Second Scrutiny; Sts Perpetua and Felicity not kept this year.
2027-02-28.prayer: O God, author of every mercy and of all goodness, who in fasting, prayer and almsgiving have shown us a remedy for sin, look graciously on this confession of our lowliness, that we, who are bowed down by our conscience, may always be lifted up by your mercy. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, zeal for your Father's house consumed you. Cleanse the temple of our hearts, drive out every idol, write your commandments on our hearts, and give the elect the living water of your Spirit. Amen.

quick: God gave the Ten Commandments to a people he had set free.
Jesus cleansed the Temple and spoke of the temple of his body.
We proclaim Christ crucified, the power and wisdom of God.

Christ crucified, the power of God.
kidsaint: A monk in Armenia, long ago, who loved to talk to God from his heart. He wrote a big book of prayers, telling God honestly about his sins and trusting God's love even more. Lesson: we can talk to God about everything, even our mistakes.
2027-02-28.special: Third Sunday of Lent. First Scrutiny of the elect; the Year A readings may be used where there are catechumens.
term: A rite celebrated with the elect on the Third, Fourth and Fifth Sundays of Lent: the community prays over them to heal what is weak and sinful and strengthen what is good, before their Baptism at Easter.

family.explain: Jesus went to the Temple, God's house, and found people buying and selling and shouting. He drove them out and said: do not make my Father's house a market! Jesus wants God's house, and our hearts too, to be places of prayer and love.
family.intention: We pray for the people who will be baptized at Easter.
family.ask: Ask: “How can we make our home and our hearts a place where Jesus is happy to stay?”

illus: A parish in Kottayam started a Lenten practice: phones in a basket at the church door, silence for ten minutes before Mass. At first people grumbled. By the Third Sunday an old man said: for years I came to church like going to the market. Now I come in and hear my own heart, and I hear God.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, zeal for your Father's house consumed you. Cleanse our hearts and make them your temple. Amen.
share: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out… of the house of slavery (Exodus 20:2). From what slavery has God freed me?
Stop making my Father's house a marketplace (John 2:16). Where do I bargain with God?
We proclaim Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 1:23). Do I find the cross foolish or powerful?
pm.resp: Lord, you have the words of everlasting life.
interc: For the elect at their First Scrutiny, that Christ may free and fill them.
For the Church, that she may be a house of prayer for all peoples.
For those enslaved by money, pleasure or addiction, that Christ may set them free.
For lawmakers, that just laws may protect life, family and the poor.
For our group, that we may keep God's commandments with love.
pm.close: Father, you gave us your Son as the true temple. Make us living stones in him. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today's first reading begins: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery (Exodus 20:2). Before God gives a single commandment, he reminds Israel: I have set you free. The Ten Commandments are not chains. They are the road map of freedom.
That is why the Psalm can say the law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul, sweeter also than honey. And we answer with Peter: Lord, you have the words of everlasting life.

In the Gospel Jesus goes into the Temple and finds a market. He makes a whip of cords, overturns the tables and says: stop making my Father's house a marketplace! (John 2:16). His disciples remember: zeal for your house will consume me.

Then he says: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up (John 2:19). He was speaking of the temple of his body. The true meeting place of God and humanity is Jesus himself, crucified and risen. And by baptism we are built into him.

St Paul says: we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to those who are the called, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:23–24). The cross looks weak, but it is stronger than all human strength.

This Lent, let Jesus walk into the temple of your heart. Let him overturn the tables where you bargain with God, drive out the idols, and make your heart a house of prayer. And let us pray for the elect at their scrutinies, that they may come to the living water at Easter. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus went to God's house and found people buying and selling and making noise. He said: this is my Father's house, a place to pray!
Our hearts are God's house too. Let us keep them clean by saying sorry and saying our prayers.

sub: A market in the house of prayer.
The Lord comes to his temple.
q: It is zeal for your house that has consumed me; the insults of those who insult you have fallen on me.

He told those who were selling the doves, “Take these things out of here! Stop making my Father's house a marketplace!” His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me.”

Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

sub: The power and wisdom of God.
q: The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the decrees of the LORD are sure, making wise the simple;
but we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to those who are the called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.

concl: God's commandments are the way of freedom; Jesus cleanses and fulfils.
The crucified and risen Body of Christ is the new temple, and we are built into it.
